metaTitle: Landscaping Advertising: Google Ads, LSA & Facebook Ads
metaDescription: Landscaping advertising run against booked jobs: Google Search Ads, Local Services Ads for lawn care and landscaping, and Facebook ads for seasonal offers.
intro: Landscaping advertising works best when each channel has one job. ASP runs Google Search Ads, Local Services Ads and Facebook ads for lawn care and landscape companies, with tracking that follows leads to booked jobs where your CRM supports it. Your ad accounts stay in your name.

sections.heading: Local Services Ads for lawn, landscape, tree and snow work
paragraphs: Google's US Local Services Ads list, checked October 2026, includes Landscaping services, Lawn care services, Tree services and Snow removal as separate categories. That gives a lawn and landscape company a pay-per-lead option in the placement that sits above the map results.

Google screens businesses before ads run. For lawn care and landscaping, its screening page lists business and owner background checks for select users, general and professional liability insurance, and state-level business and owner licenses where local law requires them. The requirements are Google's and can change.

Ranking inside Local Services Ads comes from an auction that weighs your bid and your profile quality. Google says rating, number of reviews, average response time, images and completed verification checks feed profile quality, and that missed calls may hurt responsiveness. We manage LSA against those signals, which puts review requests and answered calls on the same list as the bid.

sections.heading: Google Search Ads for the work you want more of
paragraphs: The federal definition of landscaping services includes building walkways, retaining walls, decks, fences and ponds. Search Ads are where install jobs like those get targeted by name. Each service or service area gets its own ad group with phrase match, so you can tell which service is paying, and the negative keyword list grows every week.

Our account defaults are search partners off, display off on search campaigns, location targeting set to Presence, and Max Conversions bidding until the account has the volume for a target cost per acquisition. Branded search sits in its own campaign.
Service-area businesses routinely pay for clicks outside the drive time they would accept. We compare where the spend went with where your crews want to work and tighten the targeting to match.

sections.heading: Planning ad spend around the season
paragraphs: BLS says grounds maintenance workers may be busier in spring, summer and fall, and US private employment in landscaping services ran about 34% higher in July 2024 than in January 2024. That is payroll, not lead volume, but it shows how far the trade's workforce swings within a year.

Budget and ad schedules follow your calendar. Spend leads into your busy months and pulls back when your crews are full, and companies that sell snow removal move weight to winter. After a season with tracking in place, those shifts come from your booked-job data instead of a guess.

sections.heading: Landscaping Facebook ads
paragraphs: Facebook and Instagram don't catch someone searching for a mowing service today. They keep your name in front of homeowners in your area between searches and bring back people who read your site and didn't call. Retargeting goes live before any money goes to cold audiences, because past site visitors are the cheapest audience you have.

Offers match the job. Recurring lawn care can carry a seasonal offer directly. Design and hardscape buyers take longer to decide, so those ads offer a design consultation or an estimate, backed by photos and video of projects your crews built. Stock images of somebody else's job are a common reason trade accounts underperform, and a service-area audience needs a steady supply of new creative.
Meta also helps with hiring, since the crew members you want are usually working and not browsing job boards. Recruiting runs as its own campaign with its own budget.

sections.heading: Tracking each lead to a booked job
paragraphs: Tracking gets fixed before bidding changes, because the account optimizes toward whatever it counts. The conversion action is set to the lead you sell and stays there, even if the account takes longer to leave the learning phase.

Calls get tracking numbers by source, forms pass their source into your CRM, and booked jobs get matched back to the source that produced them, where your CRM supports it. With Housecall Pro, completed jobs and their revenue can be sent back to Google Ads as offline conversions, so bidding learns from booked work instead of raw leads.
Your ad spend is paid straight to Google and Meta from accounts in your name. It isn't part of any ASP fee.

faqs.question: Can my landscaping company run Local Services Ads?
faqs.answer: When we checked in October 2026, Google's US list included categories for landscaping, lawn care, tree services and snow removal. You'll need to pass Google's screening, which for lawn care and landscaping includes liability insurance, state licenses where local law requires them, and background checks for select users. Once you're live, reviews and response time feed your ranking.

faqs.question: Do Facebook ads work for lawn care companies?
faqs.answer: For the right offer, yes. Recurring services and seasonal offers can work on Meta, and so can showing finished projects for larger installs. We start with retargeting your site visitors, because ads asking people who don't know you yet to book a service call rarely work in the trades.

faqs.question: Should I start with Google Ads or Facebook ads?
faqs.answer: Google, in almost every case. Search and Local Services Ads catch people already looking, which is the shorter path to a booked job. Facebook works best as the layer that keeps you in front of the same homeowners between searches.

faqs.question: How much should a landscaping company spend on ads?
faqs.answer: Work back from what a booked customer is worth, not from a flat monthly number. A recurring maintenance customer can be worth a full season of visits, which changes what you can afford to pay to win the first one. Ad spend goes to the platforms directly; our management fees are on the pricing page.

faqs.question: What happens to my ads in the off-season?
faqs.answer: We don't run the same budget all year. Spend pulls back when your demand drops and moves to whatever you sell in winter, such as snow removal. The account and its history stay in your name the whole time.

faqs.question: Who owns the ad accounts?
faqs.answer: You do. Your Google Ads, Local Services Ads and Meta accounts are set up in your name, with the campaign and conversion history inside them. Our what-you-own page has the full list.
